about: Reference entries. Q-codes, prosigns and abbreviations are merged in from the word lists at build time.

entries.short: Learning Morse by hearing characters at full speed from the start, adding one new character each time you copy the current set at 90% accuracy.
entries.more: Named after the German psychologist Ludwig Koch, who described it in 1936. This course uses it.

entries.short: Sending characters at a fast speed with extra space between them, so you learn the sound of each letter rather than counting dots and dashes.
Words per minute: Morse speed measured with the standard word PARIS, 50 units long.
The standard word for measuring Morse speed: exactly 50 units including the word space.
Understanding Morse in your head without writing it down, as you would listen to speech.
An operator's individual sending style: their timing, weight and rhythm, recognisable like handwriting.
A procedural signal: two letters sent run together as one character, such as AR (end of message) or SK (end of contact).
The code standardised by the ITU and used on radio worldwide, derived from Friedrich Gerke's 1848 revision of the American code.
The original landline code of Morse and Vail, with internal gaps in some letters and three dash lengths.
The Morse code for Japanese kana, switched to with the prosign DO and back with SN.
The first maritime distress call, introduced by the Marconi company in 1904, replaced by SOS.
The international distress signal, sent as one run-together character (...---...). Adopted internationally in 1906, in force from 1908.
Global Maritime Distress and Safety System: the satellite and digital system that replaced Morse for distress at sea, fully in force from 1 February 1999.
The simplest key: a lever you press for the whole of each dot and dash, so your hand forms all the timing.
A semi-automatic key: pushing the paddle one way sets a pendulum swinging that makes the dots; the other way you form each dash by hand.
A sideswiper: a key moved side to side, each direction closing the circuit, so you alternate contacts by hand. Its rhythm is distinctive.
A key with one or two levers moved sideways, used with an electronic keyer that forms the dots and dashes.
An electronic circuit that makes perfectly timed dots and dashes from a paddle.
Squeezing both paddle levers to send alternating dots and dashes. Mode A stops when you release; Mode B adds one more opposite element.
A keyer mode where squeezing both levers sends repeats of whichever lever you pressed last, instead of alternating.
The tone you hear in your headphones while sending, so you can monitor your own keying.
Full break-in: the receiver works between your dots and dashes, so the other station can interrupt you.
The transmitter switches on when you start sending and back to receive after a short pause, rather than between every element.
A keyer feature that remembers a dot paddle tap made during a dash and sends it next.
Variable frequency oscillator: the tunable oscillator that sets the frequency you transmit and receive on.
Beat frequency oscillator: mixes with a CW signal in the receiver to make it audible as a tone.
Carrier insertion oscillator: replaces the missing carrier so an SSB signal can be demodulated.
Receiver incremental tuning: shifts your receive frequency slightly without moving your transmit frequency.
Automatic gain control: turns the receiver gain down for strong signals so the volume stays even.
Automatic level control: stops the transmitter overdriving its power amplifier.
Intermediate frequency: the fixed frequency a superhet converts every signal to for filtering and gain.
Local oscillator: the oscillator a mixer combines with the incoming signal.
Superheterodyne: a receiver that converts signals to a fixed IF before filtering and detecting them.
Software-defined radio: a radio that digitises the signal early and does filtering and demodulation in software.
Analogue-to-digital converter.
Digital-to-analogue converter.
Direct digital synthesis: generating a signal by reading a stored sine wave through a DAC.
Phase-locked loop: a synthesiser that locks a VCO to a stable reference through a programmable divider.
Voltage-controlled oscillator.
Fast Fourier transform: the calculation an SDR uses to turn a signal into its spectrum.
Power amplifier: the transmitter stage that drives the antenna.
Peak envelope power: the average power over one RF cycle at the highest peak of the modulation. Licence power limits are given in PEP.
Root mean square: the AC value that gives the same heating as that much DC; 0.707 × peak for a sine wave.
Continuous wave: Morse sent by switching a carrier on and off.
Single sideband: AM with the carrier and one sideband removed. LSB below 10 MHz, USB above.
Lower sideband.
Upper sideband.
Amplitude modulation.
Frequency modulation.
Digital voice modes such as DMR, D-STAR and System Fusion.
A popular weak-signal digital mode with 15-second timed overs.
High frequency: 3–30 MHz, the bands that travel worldwide via the ionosphere.
Very high frequency: 30–300 MHz.
Ultra high frequency: 300–3000 MHz.
Radio frequency.
Alternating current.
Direct current.
Standing wave ratio: how well the antenna system matches the transmitter; 1:1 is perfect.
Antenna matching unit (often called an ATU): transforms the antenna system's impedance to 50 Ω for the transmitter.
Balanced-to-unbalanced transformer, used where coax feeds a balanced antenna such as a dipole.
A screened resistor that absorbs the transmitter's power so you can test without radiating.
Effective radiated power: the power into the antenna multiplied by its gain over a dipole.
Effective isotropic radiated power: power × gain relative to an isotropic radiator. It's 2.15 dB more than ERP.
Antenna gain relative to a half-wave dipole.
Antenna gain relative to an isotropic radiator. dBi = dBd + 2.15.
Continuous tone-coded squelch system: a sub-audible tone that opens a repeater.
A station, usually on a hilltop, that retransmits signals on another frequency to extend their range.
A converter that lets a transceiver work on another band.
Tuning so the other station's note matches your sidetone, which puts you on exactly their frequency.
The screw-on coax plug used on most HF radios.
A small bayonet coax connector.
A tiny screw-on coax connector used on handhelds.
Maximum usable frequency: the highest frequency the ionosphere will return over a given path.
Lowest usable frequency: below it, D-layer absorption makes the path unusable.
Near vertical incidence sky wave: high-angle signals that come back down nearby, for short HF contacts.
Earth–Moon–Earth: bouncing signals off the moon.
Patches of intense E-layer ionisation, mostly in summer, that open 10 m and VHF for contacts up to about 2000 km per hop.
The band of twilight round the Earth, along which low HF bands often open to far places.
The area between the end of the ground wave and where the sky wave returns, where nothing is heard.
A measure of the sun's radio output at 10.7 cm, used as a guide to HF conditions; higher is better for the high bands.
A 0–9 measure of geomagnetic disturbance; high values mean poor HF conditions.
Fading.
A distant station or contact; working DX means making long-distance contacts.
Many stations calling one (usually rare) station at once.
Transmitting on one frequency and listening on another, used by DX stations to keep callers off their frequency.
Sent by a DX station working split: call me higher up the band, as in UP 2.
The signal report: Readability 1–5, Strength 1–9, Tone 1–9. 599 is perfect.
599 with the 9s cut to N, used in contests.
Letters sent for digits to save time, such as N for 9 and T for 0.
Coordinated Universal Time, used for all log times.
A postcard (or electronic record) confirming a contact.
Amateur Data Interchange Format: the standard file format for exchanging logs.
An on-air event to make as many contacts as possible in a set time, with a short fixed exchange.
A group of three or more stations meeting on air, run by a net control station.
A formal written message passed station to station in a standard format.
A long, relaxed contact for conversation.
The agreed division of each band by mode and use.
A frequency used to make contact before moving off to talk.
A frequency where a particular mode or activity tends to gather.
Non-directional beacon: an aviation radio beacon on LF/MF that identifies itself in slow Morse.
VHF omnidirectional range: an aviation navigation beacon that sends a three-letter Morse ident on a 1020 Hz tone.
A signalling lamp with a shutter, used by ships to send Morse by light.
A grid system giving your position in a few characters, such as IO91.
Alfa, Bravo, Charlie…: words used to spell out letters clearly on voice.
The UK communications regulator, which issues amateur licences.
The Radio Society of Great Britain, the UK national society, which runs the licence exams.
The International Amateur Radio Union, which coordinates band plans across its three regions.
The International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency that allocates spectrum.
The European conference of telecoms administrations; its T/R 61-01 arrangement lets Full licensees operate temporarily in member countries.
Harmonised Amateur Radio Examination Certificate: proof of passing an exam to the CEPT standard.
The entry-level UK licence: 25 W PEP, call signs M7 and older 2E1/M3/M6.
The middle UK licence: 100 W PEP, call signs M8, M9 or older 2E0/2E1-series.
The top UK licence: up to 1 kW PEP in primary bands, recognised abroad under CEPT.
Regional Secondary Locator: the optional letter showing where you are, such as M for Scotland.
Notice of Variation: an Ofcom document that varies the terms of your licence, for example for higher power.
Status meaning amateurs have priority in a band.
Status meaning amateurs must not interfere with, and must accept interference from, primary users.
A body such as an emergency service for which amateurs may pass messages.
The United Kingdom: the area the UK licence covers also includes the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man.
Electromagnetic compatibility: equipment working without interfering with each other.
Electromagnetic field. An EMF assessment checks exposure to your station's RF fields.
International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection, whose guidance sets RF exposure limits.
UK Health Security Agency.
Protective multiple earthing: a supply system where the earth is joined to neutral, which needs care with RF earths.
Residual current breaker with overcurrent protection: trips on earth leakage as well as overload.
Residual current device: trips when current leaks to earth.
Current flowing the same way on both wires of a cable (or on the outside of coax), which a ferrite choke reduces.
The ARRL's DX Century Club award, for confirmed contacts with 100 DXCC 'entities' (countries and separate territories).
Worked All States: contacts with all 50 US states.
Worked All Zones: contacts with all 40 CQ zones.
Worked All Continents: contacts with all six continents.
Net control station: the station running a net, who calls stations in turn.
Net Q-code: I check in to the net (or, in reply, net checking-in instructions).
A call to all amateurs, used to open a net or send a bulletin.
Sent as a test signal when tuning up or checking a circuit.
One of the 40 zones CQ magazine divides the world into, used in contests and for the WAZ award.
